European leaders, pictured here with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin, Ireland last week, have stepped up efforts to end the conflict with Russia while sanctioning Moscow [File: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 17 Nov 202617 Nov 2026
Ukraine has held new talks with United States and European officials on ending the war with Russia, hours before Kyiv’s mayor reported strikes on two bridges in the capital.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Monday’s online discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and European representatives as “not easy”. But he said participants had agreed to meet in Berlin with the “Coalition of the Willing”, a group of countries supporting Ukraine, as the US and Europe step up peace talks this week.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the annual Lord Mayor's Banquet at the Guildhall in London on Monday [Jonathan Brady/Pool via Reuters]By AP and ReutersPublished On 17 Nov 202617 Nov 2026
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Brexit promise failed to deliver for the United Kingdom and that the country needs to reset its relationship with the European Union to combat growing global isolationism.
During a speech at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London on Monday, Burnham compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum, to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes”, in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked.
“I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said. “And to be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years. The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”
The remarks come ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, which Burnham said could deliver “real improvements in people’s everyday lives in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long”.
Any deal, he said, would have to pass three tests: it would have to be consistent with Labour’s manifesto and red lines, improve the Brexit deal to align with what people voted for in 2016 and pass his Makerfield Test, his benchmark for ensuring real improvements for people in parts of the UK that have long felt neglected.
The meeting is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc a decade after the UK voted to leave and six years after its 2020 departure.

An Ethiopian asylum seeker holds a child at Somare refugee camp near Moyale, along the Ethiopia-Kenya border [Baz Ratner/Reuters]By Al Jazeera staffPublished On 17 Nov 202617 Nov 2026
Moyale, Ethiopia – Fighting involving police and armed groups affiliated with Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional administrations has disrupted daily life and trade in the southern Borana Zone, as efforts to resolve a longstanding territorial dispute have yet to produce a lasting settlement.
The violence, which escalated in the border town of Moyale in October, has spread to surrounding areas, including the neighbouring districts of Arero and Wachile, leaving communities insecure and uncertain when normal life will resume.
The disruption has affected livelihoods across several parts of the zone, particularly the livestock trade – a major source of income for rural communities. Residents have reported interruptions to business activities and transport services.
A resident of Moyale town, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that people remained fearful as tensions persisted between forces affiliated with the two regional administrations.
The resident said gunfire, especially at night, had heightened personal safety concerns, while violence had restricted movement around the town and made routine activities increasingly difficult. Businesses, people raising livestock and transport operators had also been affected, leaving residents uncertain about when the situation would return to normal.
A territorial dispute reignites violence

On Monday, Judge Osmar Legal ordered Pena to be moved from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in the capital city of Asuncion.

EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas poses alongside Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani at the Techrine Palace in Damascus on September 29, 2026 [Louai Beshara/AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and ReutersPublished On 16 Nov 202616 Nov 2026
European Union foreign ministers have agreed to revive a nearly 20-year-old cooperation deal with Syria, as the bloc presses to strengthen ties with the war-scarred country.
“Syria needs investment and a successful transition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday.
“The aim is to give Europe and Syria a framework for trade, political dialogue and closer cooperation as soon as possible.”
The EU-Syria association agreement was first made in 2008 under then-President Bashar al-Assad, but it was never fully signed by either side, owing to concerns over the Assad government’s human rights record.
Kallas said EU foreign ministers meeting in Brussels had “supported moving ahead” with that deal and launching talks for an updated one.
A discussion paper prepared by the bloc’s diplomatic service ahead of the meeting outlined one of Brussels’ most ambitious efforts yet to normalise ties with Syria, less than two years after Assad’s fall.
Kallas said diplomats would now work through the technical and legal details to finalise the agreement, which would create a framework for free trade, political dialogue and broader cooperation between Brussels and Damascus.
“Everybody said that we need to engage with Syria because if we don’t engage, then this vacuum will be filled by other players,” Kallas said.
Kallas said the EU would set out new conditions for Syria to secure an updated deal.
“We should have clear conditionality regarding human rights,” she said.

Germany's Brajan Gruda celebrates [Lisi Niesner/Reuters]By Alexander HoadPublished On 16 Nov 202616 Nov 2026
An impressive Germany swept aside off-colour Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin to pip the Dutch to first place in UEFA Nations League Group A2.
Germany needed a win to stand a chance of reaching the quarterfinals, starting the night in third place behind Greece, who had won 1-0 in Germany in September, by virtue of their head-to-head record.
Jurgen Klopp’s side produced a fine attacking display to inflict the heaviest defeat on the Dutch in 67 years, as Xavi Hernandez’s side looked very ragged as they shipped four goals in 17 second-half minutes.Germany coach Jurgen Klopp on the sideline [Lisi Niesner/Reuters]
Greece’s win over Serbia left the top three sides level on 11 points, but Germany took the top spot on head-to-head while the Dutch finished second, qualifying for the last eight on goal difference thanks largely to their 7-0 win over Greece on Friday.
After a quiet opening 20 minutes, Kai Havertz headed straight at keeper Bart Verbruggen from a Joshua Kimmich free-kick, while Donyell Malen headed a Cody Gakpo cross from the left of the area over the bar from close range soon after.
Berlin-born Derry Scherhant fired a half-volley against the outside of the Dutch post on 32 minutes after collecting a cross from the right byline, but it turned out to be a range-finder as Scherhant scored his first international goal from a similar position on 44 minutes. The tech firm OpenAI has pledged more transparency after the Hugging Face cyberattack in July [File: Dado Ruvic/Illustration via Reuters]By Brian Osgood and ReutersPublished On 16 Nov 202616 Nov 2026
California has filed a lawsuit against the technology firm OpenAI, alleging that the company endangered the public by developing an artificial intelligence model without the appropriate safeguards.
The lawsuit, announced by Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday, centres on an incident that unfolded in July, when one of OpenAI’s experimental models gained access to the internet.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Australia tightens AI oversight rules after OpenAI government breachlist 2 of 3US nonprofits sue tech giants to halt AI developmentlist 3 of 3Nvidia scandal: What’s next for the US tech company?end of list
It proceeded to launch a days-long cyberattack on the AI hosting platform Hugging Face.
In the California complaint, Bonta argues that the incident indicates that OpenAI pursues growth over guardrails, leading to potentially dangerous errors.
“The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritises growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement.
The lawsuit is the first brought by a state in response to the July incident. It alleges that OpenAI violated California’s consumer protection laws and created a public nuisance through its actions.
The complaint, filed in a state court in San Francisco, calls for civil penalties against OpenAI and an injunction to bar it from engaging in actions that constitute “unfair competition”.
